clips.text_zh: 睇完即刻血壓飆升 😭 BTC 15年900倍，我喺度輸緊prop firm。15年前我得15歲啦 喂。NVDA 735倍都唔講，最慘係我連TSLA都揸唔住。仲話返美帝住大屋 先返到先再算啦。
clips.text_en_b1: $1,000 invested 15 years ago today would be worth: Bitcoin $8,970,000, Nvidia $735,000, Tesla $231,000, Apple $29,000, S&P $8,400, Gold $2,150. /biz/ today. Math hurts.
clips.source_hint: Comparison of 15-year returns across major assets

signal.rationale: Post is a hindsight comparison, no actionable trade

clips.text_en_b2: Ran the numbers on a $1,000 investment made exactly fifteen years ago, and the results are frankly brutal. Bitcoin would have ballooned to roughly $8,970,000, while Nvidia sits at around $735,000 and Tesla at $231,000. Even Apple managed $29,000, the S&P scraped by at $8,400, and gold barely moved past $2,150. Meanwhile I am grinding through a prop firm challenge, bleeding money on the daily. Math absolutely does hurt when you look at what could have been.
clips.text_en_c1: A sobering exercise in retrospective arithmetic has once again laid bare how staggeringly lucrative early positions in transformative technologies would have proven. Had one allocated a mere thousand dollars fifteen years ago, Bitcoin would have compounded into roughly nine million, Nvidia into $735,000, Tesla into $231,000, and even Apple into $29,000, while a passive S&P 500 index fund would have yielded a comparatively pedestrian $8,400 and gold merely $2,150. The /biz/ thread devolved into predictable existential anguish, with contributors lamenting that they were teenagers when generational wealth was effectively being handed away. Math, as the consensus held, hurts far more than any individual losing streak ever could.
clips.text_en_c2: A stark illustration of compounding's quiet violence: had one allocated a thousand dollars fifteen years ago, Bitcoin would now command roughly 8.97 million, Nvidia 735,000, Tesla 231,000, Apple 29,000, the S&P a meagre 8,400, and gold scarcely 2,150. The arithmetic, as any frequenter of /biz/ will attest, induces a particular kind of vertigo. One cannot help but contemplate the road not travelled: 15 at the time, ostensibly too young to act, yet old enough to have grasped what older hands fumbled. Even Nvidia's obscene multiple scarcely consoles the retail trader presently bleeding through a proprietary firm evaluation, while Tesla, that erstwhile paragon of momentum, defied every attempt at retention. The American suburban dream recedes ever further; one consoles oneself with the rhetoric of 'return first, then dream,' as if deferred gratification might yet be redeemed.

clips.text_en_b1: Redpill me on buying Cybercabs and putting them to work on the Tesla Robotaxi network for passive income. How many units would a normal retail buyer realistically need to make meaningful monthly returns?
clips.source_hint: Anon asks how to start a Cybercab Robotaxi side hustle

signal.rationale: Implicit bullish bet on Tesla Robotaxi network scaling

clips.text_en_b2: Looking for some genuine insight on the Cybercab play here, because the idea of stacking a couple of units onto Tesla's Robotaxi network for passive income sounds compelling on paper. Assuming the platform actually delivers, how many vehicles would a retail investor realistically need to clear meaningful monthly cashflow? I have not even cleared my own trading exam yet, let alone priced a fleet. Also curious where people fall on Robotaxi versus full self-driving, since they are clearly not the same bet.
clips.text_en_c1: The prospect of acquiring Cybercab units and deploying them across Tesla's forthcoming Robotaxi network has ignited considerable speculation among retail investors seeking exposure to autonomous mobility revenue streams. The underlying calculus appears deceptively straightforward: purchase vehicles at fleet pricing, register them on the platform, and collect a passive share of fares indefinitely. What remains contested, however, is the realistic threshold at which modest monthly returns become genuinely meaningful for an individual operator, given per-unit margins that may compress as supply proliferates. Whether the Robotaxi service or the underlying Full Self-Driving stack ultimately captures the lion's share of value is the question /biz/ cannot seem to settle.
clips.text_en_c2: The proposition warrants genuine scrutiny: were one to acquire a modest fleet of Cybercab units and deploy them across Tesla's nascent Robotaxi network, the residual cashflow could conceivably finance a transcontinental repatriation to American shores. The arithmetic is seductive in its symmetry, provided the underlying assumptions hold. Yet such fantasies presuppose capital that has yet to materialise; one remains, regrettably, mired in a proprietary trading evaluation, the very门槛 gating participation. Whether Robotaxi or FSD ultimately prevails is, of course, the more pertinent axis of speculation, though the distinction may prove largely academic once either achieves regulatory clearance. The optimists on /biz/ insist the barrier to scale is lower than skeptics contend; the skeptics, conversely, decry the optimists as credulous. Between these poles, the prudent retail observer simply waits.

clips.text_en_b1: OpenAI just launched GPT-6 Astra and said welcome to the AGI era. The benchmarks are wild. It nearly saturates ARC-AGI 3. The strongest model ever released, according to the company itself.
clips.source_hint: OpenAI announces flagship GPT-6 Astra model

signal.rationale: Tech news observation, no trade setup

clips.text_en_b2: OpenAI has officially rolled out GPT-6 Astra, and the company is not being shy about calling it the AGI era, which honestly makes my blood run cold. The benchmarks are genuinely wild, with the model nearly saturating ARC-AGI 3, and OpenAI themselves are touting it as the most capable system they have ever shipped. If AI is already closing in on surveying work, then what exactly am I grinding certification exams for at this point?
clips.text_en_c1: OpenAI's unveiling of GPT-6 Astra, accompanied by the company's unequivocal declaration that we have formally entered the AGI era, has predictably sent shockwaves through technology circles. Internal benchmarks suggest the system approaches saturation on ARC-AGI 3, a metric that until recently had remained stubbornly resistant to frontier-scale models, prompting the company to characterise it as the most capable architecture ever released to the public. For white-collar professionals whose workflows overlap with what the model now demonstrably handles, the announcement lands less as a milestone and more as an ominous inflection point, accelerating anxieties that have been building for several product cycles.
clips.text_en_c2: OpenAI has formally unveiled GPT-6 under the codename Astra, heralding what its leadership rather grandiloquently terms 'the AGI era,' a rhetorical flourish that, if substantiated, renders the remainder of one's professional trajectory somewhat precarious. The benchmarks, as circulated across /g/, are genuinely staggering: the model reportedly saturates ARC-AGI 3 to a degree that would have seemed implausible mere quarters ago, and the company, never shy of superlatives, deems it the strongest system yet released. One's surveying credentials, painstakingly accrued over years of examination purgatory, now appear destined for obsolescence before their ink has dried. The existential arithmetic is unforgiving: if artificial cognition can perform the cognitive labour itself, what precisely remains for the human surveyor? Welcome, indeed, to the era.

clips.text_en_b1: Anons on /pol/ ranting about Finland. They land in Helsinki, Tampere, Oulu, even Rovaniemi, and everywhere has migrants and Indians now. Typical /pol/ meltdown but the underlying complaint is housing and crowding.
clips.source_hint: Anon complains about migration across Finnish cities
clips.text_en_b2: The /pol/ thread is once again melting down over European migration, and although the framing is predictably right-wing, there is a kernel of truth underneath the rant. Anons claim migrants and Indians are showing up everywhere from Helsinki and Tampere down to Oulu and even Rovaniemi, while housing gets tighter by the month. Beneath all the culture-war posturing, the real grievance keeps circling back to overcrowding and runaway property prices, which is frankly a feeling I understand far better than I would like.
clips.text_en_c1: The latest /pol/ fixation on Finland has devolved into the customary meltdown, with anonymous posters lamenting that migrants and Indian nationals now seem omnipresent from the comparatively cosmopolitan streets of Helsinki through Tampere, Oulu, and even the Arctic confines of Rovaniemi. Beneath the unsavoury rhetoric, however, lies a grievance that transcends ideology: a pervasive sense that housing markets have become untenable, public infrastructure is stretched to breaking point, and the social fabric that once defined Nordic homogeneity is fraying under demographic pressure. Whether one sympathises with the framing or not, the underlying complaint about crowding carries a legitimacy that deserves more measured engagement.
clips.text_en_c2: The denizens of /pol/ have, with characteristic fury, descended upon Finland as their latest exhibit in the perennial European migration thesis. The argument, stripped of its more inflammatory ornamentation, proceeds thus: the migrants and Indians are everywhere now, in Tampere, in Oulu, even in Rovaniemi, and the native Finnish fabric is accordingly being threadbare. Beneath the customary /pol/ hysteria lies a more pedestrian grievance, namely housing scarcity and the particular claustrophobia of small cities groaning beneath demographic pressure. One recognises, if reluctantly, the underlying sentiment; Hong Kong itself grows ever more congested, every district thronged, every carriage packed. The dream of American suburban spaciousness persists as the consolation, even as the practical pathways thereto narrow with each passing quarter and each tightening immigration regime.

clips.text_en_b2: Somehow an eroge has knocked every AAA release out of the top spot on Steam Japan, and the fact that it outsold the entire competitive slate on PC is honestly hilarious. The Japanese market clearly stays loyal to its niche interests, regardless of what the rest of the industry is hyping. Personally I have not even had time to touch League this season, although once exams are done I will finally get around to actually playing something again.
clips.text_en_c1: In what can only be described as a quietly triumphant vindication of niche Japanese PC gaming, an eroge has unseated every major AAA contender to claim the top spot on Steam's Japan regional charts, outselling even the most heavily marketed Western blockbusters. The result, while unsurprising to seasoned observers of the domestic PC market, nonetheless underscores a peculiarity that continues to perplex international analysts: Japanese consumers maintain a ferocious loyalty to genres and conventions that global publishers consistently misjudge or ignore. The /v/ thread oscillated between amused resignation and outright celebration, treating the outcome as further evidence that mainstream gaming discourse remains woefully out of touch.
clips.text_en_c2: In a development that has occasioned considerable mirth among /v/'s more contrarian posters, the Japanese Steam charts have been topped, quite decisively, by an eroge, whose sales have eclipsed those of any AAA competitor within the Japanese PC market. The Japanese PC gaming demographic, it must be conceded, exhibits a loyalty to its niche genres that Western publishers consistently underestimate; the otaku demographic that sustains this market is neither casual nor ephemeral, but rather fiercely devoted. One observes this development with the detached amusement of someone whose own gaming hours have dwindled to near-zero, League of Legends season 5 largely unwatched, anime backlog eternally postponed. The faithful companion in such matters remains the chubby correspondent, whose invitations to congregate around shared viewing constitute, in their modest way, the remaining social infrastructure of the modern shut-in.

clips.text_zh: 笑死 /fit/啲人個個都cut到lift跌 然後勁多excuses 😂 shoulder痛 換grip 喺客廳練⋯⋯ 我都係 膊頭真係廢 脂肪再低啲會好啲。
clips.text_en_b1: Classic /fit/ copypasta. Cutting, so bench is down. Bad shoulders, so no squat. Living room lifts, so numbers down. Narrow grip, no leg drive, low reps to recover shoulders while cutting, then supposedly back to heavy. Every excuse in the book.
clips.source_hint: Anon lists every bench plateau excuse imaginable
clips.text_en_b2: The classic /fit/ cutting copypasta has surfaced once again, and the excuses are frankly a work of literature at this point. Bad shoulders mean no squatting, the bench is down because of course it is, and since the lifter is stuck doing living room curls the numbers are obviously tanked. Throw in a narrow grip, zero leg drive, and low reps to nurse the shoulders through the cut, and somehow heavy triples are allegedly waiting on the other side.
clips.text_en_c1: The quintessential /fit/ copypasta has resurfaced once again, and its particulars remain grimly familiar to anyone who has spent meaningful time in the board's archives. The poster, currently in a caloric deficit, finds their bench press numbers in steady decline; their shoulders preclude any meaningful squat volume; and the constraints of training in a cramped living room further compromise the integrity of every working set. Narrow grip, abandoned leg drive, and deliberately truncated rep ranges are all rationalised as temporary concessions that will allegedly evaporate once the cut concludes and the sacred return to heavy triples resumes.
clips.text_en_c2: The /fit/ cutting copypasta has assumed the quality of liturgy, its recitation now more ritualistic than sincere. Bench press declines precipitously, but the shoulders, naturally, preclude any compensatory squat work; one trains in the living room, where the absence of proper equipment necessarily diminishes the loads one can move; the narrow grip, eschewing the leg drive that might otherwise elevate the numbers, permits only low-rep sets that ostensibly safeguard the recovering shoulders. Once the cut concludes, one will purportedly return to heavy compounds, though this prophesied restoration has, for many a poster, remained perpetually deferred across successive cutting phases. The taxonomy of excuses is comprehensive: every conceivable malady, every plausible contrivance, every physiological alibi is marshalled in defence of numbers that, frankly, were never particularly impressive in the first place.

clips.text_en_b1: Demon Slayer / Kimetsu no Yaiba, watching for the first time, now on season 2. Why do so many people hate on it? Most criticisms apply equally to other beloved anime, but this one made billions, so it gets targeted.
clips.source_hint: Newcomer defends Demon Slayer against haters
clips.text_en_b2: Finally got around to watching Demon Slayer and I am now midway through season two, which honestly holds up far better than I expected. The question that keeps nagging, however, is why this franchise in particular draws so much hatred, since most of the criticisms people level at it apply just as easily to plenty of beloved titles. My take is that once something makes billions, it inevitably becomes a target, and anime fans can be unusually tribal about commercial success.
clips.text_en_c1: Demon Slayer, otherwise known as Kimetsu no Yaiba, has finally crossed into my viewing rotation, and having progressed into its second season, I find myself genuinely perplexed by the disproportionate hostility the series routinely attracts online. The standard criticisms levelled against it, ranging from derivative narrative structures to occasionally underwhelming antagonists, could just as readily be applied to a slew of venerated shounen properties that enjoy far more forgiving critical treatment. The conclusion, however unwelcome to its detractors, appears inescapable: commercial success on the scale of multiple billions invites a particular brand of contrarian backlash that artistic merit alone cannot insulate a franchise from, however unfair that dynamic may ultimately…
clips.text_en_c2: Kimetsu no Yaiba, otherwise known as Demon Slayer, has proven, upon belated first viewing, a thoroughly competent shounen production; one finds oneself, somewhat to one's own surprise, now well into the second season, genuinely engaged by its set-piece choreography if occasionally fatigued by its narrative pacing. The question that persists, however, is the curious one of reception: why does this particular property attract such disproportionate scorn? Critics apply standards to it that they conspicuously decline to apply to comparably beloved contemporaries, and the suspicion is inescapable that commercial success itself constitutes the provocation, that a series amassing billions must, by some inverted logic, be punished for its popularity.
